node.label: Gertrude Himmelfarb
node.date_label: The Idea of Poverty (1984) · The New History and the Old (1987; revised 2004) · Poverty and Compassion (1991)
node.description: In The Idea of Poverty (1984), Gertrude Himmelfarb studied poverty as a changing moral and political idea, connecting social conditions with how contemporaries understood them. Poverty and Compassion (1991) argued that the material and moral dimensions of poverty were inseparable in the minds of late Victorians. The New History and the Old (1987) defended political and intellectual inquiry against the displacement she attributed to newer historical approaches. Her defense provoked disagreement: Lawrence Stone accepted some objections but disputed the claimed dominance of new history, and David Cannadine later rejected her diagnosis of disciplinary ruin. Her methodological essays criticized quantitative history as deterministic and psychohistory as lacking evidence, and later defended evidentiary method against postmodern accounts of historical knowledge.
node.representative_figures_and_works: The Idea of Poverty: England in the Early Industrial Age (1984); The New History and the Old (1987; revised edition 2004); Poverty and Compassion: The Moral Imagination of the Late Victorians (1991); “Tradition and Creativity in the Writing of History” (1992).
node.scope_note: Selected sections of the 1975 article, the complete 1992 First Things essay, selected Stone and Nisbet review passages, and Cannadine’s opening pp. 29–33 were read. Selected books are known through publisher description, bibliography and named reviewers; none was read in full. Scott’s 1989 interventions, Valverde’s 1992 review, the 1989 Reflections article and the separate 1992 TLS essay remain unread. Interlocutors’ originals were not newly read.

proposed_edges.relationship: In ‘Tradition and Creativity in the Writing of History’ (1992), Himmelfarb criticizes White’s treatment of historical writing through literary forms.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Read paragraphs beginning ‘Hayden White’ and ‘For the postmodernist’; ‘Poetics of History’. White’s originals unread; records her interpretation.

proposed_edges.relationship: In ‘Tradition and Creativity in the Writing of History’ (1992), Himmelfarb challenges Scott’s linkage of feminist history with poststructuralist epistemology.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Read ‘The political potential’ through ‘If conventional history’; ‘radical epistemology’. Scott’s original passage unread; criticism remains Himmelfarb’s.

proposed_edges.relationship: In ‘Resisting the New’ (1987), Stone disputes Himmelfarb’s exaggerated account of new history’s dominance while accepting some objections.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Read review paragraphs ‘All this granted’ through ‘Thus outside France’; ‘overstates a good case’. Reviewed book unread; qualified criticism.

proposed_edges.relationship: In ‘What is History Now?’ (2004), Cannadine rejects Himmelfarb’s diagnosis of disciplinary ruin, arguing that political history remains vigorous.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Read official PDF, printed pp. 31–32, paragraph crossing the page break and note 10: ‘political history remains alive and well’. Lecture delivered 2002; published text 2004, not all wording backdated. Cited Himmelfarb books unread.

proposed_edges.relationship: In The New History and the Old (1987), Himmelfarb criticizes Braudel’s account of individual freedom, as Stone reports.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Read Stone’s paragraph ‘One of Himmelfarb’s beliefs’; ‘efficacy of individuals’. Both original book discussions unread; mediated criticism only.

proposed_edges.relationship: In ‘Tradition and Creativity in the Writing of History’ (1992), Himmelfarb defends evidentiary checks against what she calls postmodern relativism.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Read ‘Critical history put a premium’ and concluding methodological defense; ‘canon of evidence’. Her contested position, not a disciplinary verdict.

proposed_edges.relationship: In The New History and the Old (1987), Himmelfarb criticizes quantitative history as deterministic and mechanistic and singles out cliometricians such as Robert Fogel, as Stone reports.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Read ‘Again, however’ through ‘Here the historian’ and ‘To barzun’ through ‘But in these cases’; ‘for whom it is a method’. Fogel and Engerman are joint authors. Their book and Barzun’s book unread; objection concerns explanatory sufficiency, not all counting.

proposed_edges.relationship: In The New History and the Old (1987), Himmelfarb dismisses psychohistories, including Erikson’s study of Luther, as unscholarly for lacking historical evidence, as Lawrence Stone reports.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Lawrence Stone, “Resisting the New,” New York Review of Books, 17 December 1987, paragraph beginning She lists the types of new social history, and the following sentences naming Erikson’s Luther study and describing her dismissal as unscholarly for lack of evidence. Stone does not supply the book title. This is his account of the 1987 collection; the collection and the psychohistorical studies remain unread.

proposed_edges.relationship: In The New History and the Old (1987), Himmelfarb criticizes social history’s fragmentation and displacement of political inquiry, as Stone reports.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Read Stone’s ‘She also sees’ and following paragraph; ‘factional and parochial’. Collection unread; attribution preserves disagreement.

proposed_edges.relationship: The Idea of Poverty (1984) makes changing conceptions of poverty a historical problem, joining social and intellectual history in Nisbet’s reading.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Read Nisbet’s opening, especially paragraphs ‘Style’ through ‘The important characters’: ‘social history’ and ‘intellectual history’. Book unread; contribution framed through this named reviewer, without treating his favorable assessment as consensus.
proposed_edges.map_label: Studies poverty as a historical idea

proposed_edges.relationship: In her review “Sire of the Poor” (1988), Linda Colley questioned the claim in Gertrude Himmelfarb’s Victorian Values and 20th-Century Condescension (1987) that Victorian England shared a consensual value system across social groups.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Read the publisher-hosted review, including its discussion of Himmelfarb and the contrasting studies by Read and Anderson. Colley accepts that some workers embraced the virtues under discussion, but questions generalizing that agreement across Victorian society. This records reception through criticism, not adoption. The pamphlet itself was not read.
proposed_edges.map_label: Questions a shared Victorian value system

proposed_edges.relationship: In “A Neo-Victorian Romance” (1987), Keith Thomas criticized Gertrude Himmelfarb’s Marriage and Morals Among the Victorians (1986) for selective portraits of Bentham, Bloomsbury and the Webbs and for judging past thinkers without sufficiently situating them in their own contexts.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Read the publisher-hosted review. Thomas praises the essays’ literary qualities while challenging their selection of evidence and historical contextualization. The claim is limited to this review; the collection was not read. Its 1986 publication year is corroborated by the publisher excerpt of T. G. Otte’s The Foreign Office Mind, introduction p. 10, note 44.
proposed_edges.map_label: Challenges selective portraits and missing context
